Poverty stays where it is.

Building density — a satellite proxy for local prosperity — is almost perfectly persistent across 12 countries: where a place sits in 2016 all but determines 2023, and poverty is tightly clustered in space. Yet the landscape splits into two basins — empty and settled — the signature of a spatial poverty trap.

Where poverty is

Building density, ranked into deciles — 2023 and 2016

Each country's hexes ranked 1 (sparsest) → 10 (densest). Cities blaze bright; arid and riverine fringes stay dark. The two maps are near-identical — the poverty map barely changes in seven years.

Persistence & trap — the four tests

One tight trajectory, two basins of settlement

Bangladesh, worked through the four diagnostics: (1) time persistence, (2) spatial persistence, (3) the negative-growth trap test, (4) the density distribution — bimodal (empty vs settled), the two-steady-states signature.

National Bangladesh hexes, 2016→2023 (asinh, zeros kept).
Does space matter?

Poverty is clustered — but neighbours predict you only loosely

Neighbours' density (2023) vs your own (2023). Clear spatial clustering, but far weaker than own-persistence — on the same scale this diagonal is lighter than the one above. That gap is why a neighbour's density makes a strong but invalid instrument: relevant, yet confounded by shared geography.

P(own rank 2023 | neighbour rank 2023), per country. Same colour scale as the persistence figure.
